rv.q: But it’s a remarkable end to an extraordinary play.

It’s bracing to see someone use the stage with such emphatic intent to provoke discourse, and Rodrigues draws on writers as varied as Aeschylus, Lorca, Brecht and Shaw to work up his unique, disturbing brew.
But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing
A striking premise, then, but as happens in the story itself, it feels as though the execution itself gets botched.

This kind of declamatory agitprop went out with the Ark (or at least the 1970s), and what might have been genuinely inflammatory – putting out fire with gasoline – is closer to the damp, smouldering embers of rain-soaked barbecue.
To the credit of this extraordinary and so, so timely production, I'm now further away than ever from knowing if it's if or when and then comes the even more terrifying interrogative, how?
This remains urgent, provocative stuff – exactly the sort of thing the National should be programming.
This production is nuanced, unsettling and thoughtful.
It’s a tough and drawn-out watch in sections, but has there ever been a more contentious and apposite vehicle for the times in which we live?
But there’s an uncomfortable sense that by setting out to trigger a reaction, it is a little too sure of its own importance.
Provocative if also heavy-handed Portuguese drama pays a welcome visit to London.
All the Catarinas are fully-formed characters, with João Vicente’s nascent capitalist Catarina a particular delight.
The writing feels as though you could hand-pick almost any line at random and find something intense, daring and beautifully provocative.
If theatre at its best has the power to make you think and feel, Catarina… is the perfect example of this.
An example of unforgettable theatre that delivers mixed results.
Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists confronts questions of political engagement and tactics of resistance head-on.

cn.t: Rodrigues' provocative Portuguese import divides critics with its confrontational approach to fascism. While some praise its urgent, bracingly powerful examination of political violence, others find it heavy-handed and tediously long.

ru.inst: Released Fridays at 1 PM via the National Theatre website (random queue).
